name: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis
lead: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique that lengthens the lower jaw gradually. The bone is cut and the segments are slowly separated by a device, so new bone forms in the gap.[7][8] The principle derives from Ilizarov's work on long bones, who showed bone forms when stretched along its axis at about 1 mm per day.[3]

The modern clinical era in the jaw is dated to 1992 reports of gradual mandibular lengthening by McCarthy and colleagues.[7] A 1995 report described an oblique corticotomy technique used in 87 patients.[1] Its best-documented uses are in mandibular hypoplasia such as hemifacial microsomia and Treacher Collins syndrome, and in infants with micrognathia and airway obstruction, such as in Pierre Robin sequence.[2][6][9][10]

Published evidence is mostly case series and cohort reports in children with congenital conditions. In looksmaxxing culture it is mentioned among procedures for adults seeking mandibular advancement; the sources reviewed describe no studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity.

paras: The phases are osteotomy with device placement, a latency of about a week, activation at roughly 1 mm per day, and consolidation before the device is removed in a second operation.[7] Devices can be external frames, which allow monitoring but carry pin-site infection and scarring risk, or buried intraoral distractors, which reduce those risks but demand accurate planning.[8] One summary gives mandibular advancements of about 10-24 mm.[8]

Biological work in animals has shown that blood vessel formation and the mechanical environment are required for bone induction during distraction.[4] A 2018 mouse study reported that mechanoresponsive stem cells acquire neural crest fate in jaw regeneration.[5]

Studies have examined distraction to relieve upper airway obstruction in young children with craniofacial deformities,[2][10] including in neonates as a strategy to avoid tracheostomy[9] and as part of an algorithm for isolated Pierre Robin sequence.[11] A 2001 study of ten patients aged 3 months to 8 years measured airway cross-sectional area changes.[2] Reviews of infant sleep apnea discuss obstructive causes.[12]

A 2001 review of 3,278 craniofacial distraction cases is a major source on complications.[13] Wikipedia summarizes figures of about 5% infection, 7-9% bone growing in an unintended direction, 3-4.5% hardware failure, and in mandibular distraction about 3.5% inferior alveolar nerve damage, 2% tooth bud injury and 0.5% facial nerve injury.[7] Another summary reports pin-site infection in roughly 6-27% of sites and reports that complication rates fall with surgeon experience.[8]

Human evidence includes the 87-patient 1995 series,[1] the 2001 ten-patient airway study,[2] and the 3,278-case review.[13] Registered studies include computer-guided distraction in hemifacial microsomia (n=12),[14] CAD/CAM surgical templates for mandible distraction (n=30),[15] and a comparison of internal and external distractors (n=30).[16] No studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity were found.

card.summary: Gradual lower-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, well documented in children with congenital conditions, unstudied for purely cosmetic use.
card.note: Evidence is from congenital and airway cases; nerve injury and infection are documented complications.

quick.overview:
Mandibular distraction cuts the lower jaw and slowly stretches the gap with a device so new bone forms. It is established for children with small jaws and airway obstruction, such as Pierre Robin sequence.

The literature is mainly case series and cohort reports; no studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity were found.
quick.mechanism: After a cut and a week-long latency, the device lengthens the jaw at about 1 mm per day, followed by a consolidation period as bone matures. Devices can be external or internal.
quick.risks: A large review of 3,278 craniofacial cases documents complications; summaries report infection, hardware failure, and inferior alveolar nerve, tooth bud or facial nerve injury in a minority of cases.
